nameStory: Yellow stonecrop gets its name from its bright golden-yellow flowers and its incredible ability to thrive on stones and rocky surfaces where other plants would quickly perish. The word 'stonecrop' comes from the Old English meaning 'stone crop' - a plant that can literally 'crop up' from seemingly barren stone. It's like nature's little rock garden specialist!
description: Yellow stonecrop is a low-growing succulent that forms neat, compact mounds of fleshy green leaves. This charming little plant rarely grows more than 6 inches tall but can spread outward to create attractive ground-covering patches. In spring, it bursts into bloom with clusters of bright yellow, star-shaped flowers that seem to glow against the green foliage. Originally from Japan and Korea, this hardy little survivor has found its way into New England gardens and occasionally escapes into the wild.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow, star-shaped flowers with 5 pointed petals arranged in dense, flat-topped clusters. The flowers feel papery to the touch and have a subtle, sweet fragrance that attracts small pollinators.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, fleshy leaves that feel rubbery and smooth when squeezed, storing water like tiny green balloons. They're bright green, oval-shaped, and arranged in opposite pairs along the stems.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mounds that hug the ground, rarely exceeding 6 inches tall. The stems trail along the surface and root at nodes, creating dense mats.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: The entire plant has a distinctive succulent feel - leaves and stems are plump and squishy when gently pressed, like squeezing a grape. This watery texture is unmistakable among New England plants.

habitat: In New England, yellow stonecrop is primarily found in cultivated settings like rock gardens, stone walls, and xeriscaped areas where it's been planted for ground cover. It occasionally escapes cultivation and can establish on thin, rocky soils, stone walls, and well-drained slopes where few other plants can survive. Look for it in sunny, dry locations with excellent drainage.

seasonality.spring: Bright yellow star-shaped flowers appear in dense clusters, typically blooming from late spring into early summer. This is when the plant is most noticeable and easiest to identify.
seasonality.summer: After flowering, the plant focuses on vegetative growth, spreading via trailing stems. The thick, fleshy green leaves remain prominent and diagnostic throughout the growing season.
seasonality.fall: Foliage may take on reddish or bronze tints as temperatures cool. The succulent leaves remain plump and green longer than most plants as they prepare for dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground in harsh New England winters, leaving only the root system alive underground to regenerate in spring.

funFact: Yellow stonecrop can survive being completely dried out for weeks - if you accidentally pull up a piece and leave it on a rock, it might still be alive and ready to replant a month later, thanks to the massive amount of water stored in its balloon-like leaves!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Kamchatka stonecrop, its close cousin that also has yellow flowers and succulent leaves. The key difference is that yellow stonecrop forms more compact, tighter mounds while Kamchatka stonecrop tends to be more sprawling and loose in its growth habit.
contextualKnowledge: This plant was formerly classified as a Sedum and you may still see it sold in nurseries under names like Sedum ellacombianum. Botanists recently moved it to the genus Phedimus, but gardeners and many plant labels haven't caught up with this change yet.
compareHints: Among its Phedimus relatives in New England, yellow stonecrop is distinguished by its compact, mounded growth habit and consistently bright yellow spring flowers. Caucasian stonecrop has pink or red flowers, while hybrid stonecrop shows variable flower colors. Kamchatka stonecrop, its closest look-alike, has a more sprawling, less tidy growth pattern and slightly larger individual flowers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its stonecrop relatives, Caucasian stonecrop is distinguished by its opposite leaf arrangement and two-ranked growth pattern (leaves in two rows).
Hybrid Stonecrop has noticeably larger, more paddle-shaped leaves than its relatives like Caucasian Stonecrop, which has smaller, more rounded leaves.

Among its Phedimus relatives in New England, Kamchatka Stonecrop stands out for its distinctly orange-tinted flowers - Caucasian Stonecrop has purer yellow or pinkish blooms, while other related species tend toward bright yellow or white.

Aizoon Stonecrop differs from its Phedimus relatives by having the most prominently toothed leaf margins - those little saw teeth are much more pronounced than in Caucasian Stonecrop or Kamchatka Stonecrop.
